Comment:
Idk, I see myself in that post. There are many lessons I had to learn because I love to joke as well.

1) You have to build up trust before joking. People don’t know you yet and your conduct can come off as inappropriate if you joke too much with strangers. It can also be perceived as “getting too comfortable” when you start poking or taking shots to laugh (depending on how you deliver jokes). You start looking like you lack respect and boundaries.

2) Being too charming (funny or flirty) is not a substitute for intimacy. I used to be very charming but wouldn’t be appropriately vulnerable when the moment came. I didn’t lead with empathy and care at the start, so trust wasn’t built.

3) Building a connection with humor as opposed to real intimacy is a false connection. It feels warm and fun, but it isn’t real connection. Real connection involves vulnerability and seeing others in a different light to develop empathy and as such, connection.

4) don’t use people as the joke until trust has developed and they know you’re a good mores on and mean no harm. It can be fun to pick on each other and be silly, but without built trust, you risk hurting the other person. Go slow at the start.

Comment: Obviously, your socially anxious version is also you (a part of you), but that's not the point. The point is that your guards are so high up that it blocks your any kind of vulnerable side all together. And we know very well that genuine connection comes from taking on the risk of some level of vulnerability. Like, taking the risk of making a joke, and maybe crossing the line a bit, then apologizing, then adjusting your jokes for the next time. So, your socially anxious version is certainly a version of you, but it's not the "you" you can have genuine connection with other people. It's a fight-flight-freeze version suitable for much more dangerous situations, to protect you from immense harm. You don't have to be totally relaxed like at home. But if you totally block your inner, relaxed personality, social life becomes hell, and in a way, that's not really you. So saying "I can't be myself" is basically correct.

Comment: I guess it makes sense if by saying "social anxiety is your personality" you mean "your brain is wired a certain way that makes you have an anxious reaction in social situations by activating the sympathetic system, and you can re-wire it with enough work". However, I think what most people mean when they talk about being their "real selves" is the way thay behave when the parasympathetic system is in act. I know they both are parts of our nervous system and that my anxious behavior in certain situations is not completely separate from what I perceive as my real self. But it is helpful to understand that this reaction doesn't define me, and it is something that can change depending on the level of stress I'm experiencing. For me the social anxiety usually shows up only when there's a reason for me to feel uncomfortable in certain group of people, and it almost disappears in other situations and groups, even if I don't know these people closely. What I'm trying to say is, the circumstances that cause stress may be different for everybody, but when that stress breakpoint is reached, your reaction would always feel like you're acting not as your normal self, and it's valid to feel this way, because it's true that as soon as that factor is removed, you feel like you again.

	•	Social anxiety is not only an internal experience; it actively shapes how other people treat me, especially how honest they are with me.

Making Yourself Small & Obsequiousness

Author: @DogOnAKeyboard
Comment:
Back in like high school or around there, I used to have so much social anxiety, I remember one instance in like a book cafe. But it was like I was already making up in my mind that everyone was watching or looking at me and thinking I'm weird or making a judgement. I could hardly look anyone in the eyes or feel comfortable even just looking around me to assess my own assumptions. What helped me in that time is to lean into the discomfort and challenge myself to actually look around the room. I was nervous to do it and heart was elevated, but what I found is very few if any people ever were looking at me in the way I had imagined. I realized my perception and projection really skewed how I felt in those moments. So I kept practicing that until that kind of evaporated because it was based more on a fear that I imagined happening than what really was happening. If anyone glanced up at me, it was just a neutral or curious expression.
Now I don't experience social anxiety in that way or with that degree. :D Don't get me wrong, I still hate doing group presentations, but existing in just social environments or with people around doesn't feel so threatening.

I had the exact same problem in my early twenties. What you are experiencing is a run away phobia that morphs into fear of being fearful. There are ways around it. 1. Medications such as beta blockers or anti anxiety meds. 2. Start getting interested in other people instead of trying to perform- meaning ask engaging questions. People love to talk about themselves and like people that are good listeners 3. Also exposure therapy - get in these situations often and once in a while try to make mistakes. It trains you to learn that you won't die from saying something stupid. 4. Admit the problem- tell trusted associates that you are nervous in a group setting. Or that are fearful of public speaking. 

The root of the problem isnt the anxiety but rather the fear of being found out. 

You will gradually overcome it, and it will cease to be an issue.

Author: @ascenshua
Comment:
Training your perception is so frustrating to learn, because you're essentially learning to question everything you've habitually gotten used to your whole life and things that you will come across. For me it boils down to: "what do I believe to be true that might not be?" This means you have to learn what exactly your habits/immediate thoughts are, and then to challenge them. One of the ways to do that is videos like these that show you other ways to think about issues, but another is to also have data that isn't your own through asking others. This also means that there are certain parts of yourself whose opinions actually can't be relied on yet.

I know a friend that was often bullied and verbally abused when they were younger, so they lived a life turned inward, reclused, and also jealous of others' successes. This friend became highly self-conscious, socially anxious, often depressed, and had a hard time being confident and believing they could succeed. They thought they could predict others' emotions and thoughts in any social situation, but I think this was just a way for my friend to protect themselves from the threat of perceived bullying. The problem was their "predictions" were often negative in nature, often self-defeating and highlighting the bad parts of themselves. They would constantly question if people hated them if a recent social event went south. It was honestly so self-absorbed and one-sided, and the most annoying part was that it was so sure of itself despite completely missing information. When I talked to other people's perspectives on this, they didn't think the same things my friend did about themselves and often saw things in a neutral or positive light. My friend's beliefs of themselves were convinced to the point that their life was going to go a negative way and the constant deliberating made them turn inwards more and more to the point where trying to dig out of it felt like it would just cave-in again. 

I hope everyone watching this video questions their own understandings about themselves. In my experience, it takes effort and hurt but is probably the only way to ever see meaningful change in life.
